78.t: Don Redman as bandleader: thorough rehearsals and quick voicings
78.s: Redman knew music thoroughly and rehearsed arrangements until memorized; he voiced chords instantly by assigning notes to each horn.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: Don was excellent to work with. In fact, he knew everything in music that you wanted to know about music. You would ask him questions about how you would phrase things, and, of course, Don played the alto saxophone in his

78.t: Lucky Millinder: a conductor with a great ear who couldn't read
78.s: Millinder could not read music but learned riffs after hearing a rehearsal and conducted with a baton; Horace wrote him 'Hallelujah'.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: Lucky Millender. Now that's a guy that was a real character. When I say character, I mean he was funny. I could tell you some stories on Lucky Millender.

251.s: Nobody missed rehearsals. The book held 150 to 200 numbered arrangements, in one folder per man, and the players knew the numbers by heart.
251.q: They were more interested in rehearsing than they were doing in anything else, especially when they would get a new arrangement. There was no problem in the call rehearsal. They'd be up all night and get up and rehearse again.

12.t: Rehearsing new arrangements and memorising them
12.s: Process of learning new numbers by sections and memorising, with Armstrong's memory.
12.q: Well, you'd get used to them, yeah. You'd get used to them, sure. We'd take, when we came off the road from the least one night, as we'd go on the road saying, Joe Green would build a tune for us for two months. The Easton tune, the Western tune, and the Southern tune, and all that sort of stuff.…

121.t: Rehearsing for new singers and simpler music
121.s: They learned singers' hits or got song lists; music was simpler, like Joe Turner finding his key.
121.ch: The Dew Drop, Blue Eagle and visiting stars
121.q: Yeah, well, either we'd have a rehearsal or we knew that particular singer's songs that they would do. We would get a list of the songs that they would do, or they hit record, they had a hit record, we learned a hit record, and just go from there. You know, because for some reason the music was a…

200.s: Players sang, memorised and noted parts in dots and dashes; parts changed daily and with each added player, so missing a rehearsal left you lost.
200.q: He’d have you either sing it, play it and memorize it, and then change it. After you remember your parts he’d give you another one.

691.t: Joining Al Vollmer's Harlem Blues and Jazz Band
691.s: Subbing for the band's singer after Terry Waldo's show; no rehearsals; advice on being ready.
691.q: I was doing a show with a gentleman named Terry Waldo, who specializes in ragtime music and all the old tunes. And he studied with Eubie Blake and I think he worked on some of his music categorizing it or cataloguing it. And Terry was doing a show where Shea Stadium was, the old World’s Fair was…

450.s: The trio rehearsed informally at Dave's apartment and polished by performing; she sang trumpet or piano parts, Jon tenor and Dave trombone.
450.q: It was called doing it as you did it. We never — we would get together, I’d walk in with that many newspapers, I was a newspaper freak. Jon would be doing a crossword puzzle, Dave would be putting things on paper and voicing, at Dave’s little apartment in the Village And he’d say okay, let’s try…

4.t: Make-up bands and the thirty tunes everybody knew
4.s: Bands were assembled from whoever was available because everyone knew twenty-five or thirty standards without rehearsal.
4.ch: Later ventures, lodges and San Francisco recollections
4.q: A good saxophone player--he knew a piano player, and he'd get...we'd call him, and he'd get a piano player and a drummer and a trumpet... whatever it with. Sometimes some guy'd be playing--if he wasn't working tonight, he'd get on this job. If he wasn't...tomorrow night, if you need him, he'd be on…

9.t: Sunday matinee dances and head arrangements at the Saratoga
9.s: The empty club filled for Sunday matinees; the band hardly rehearsed and played mostly head arrangements with Red Allen fitting in.
9.q: Oh, we played. We played down there. Every Sunday they would have a matinee dance. The place would be packed and jammed. Every Sunday afternoon. The rest of the week, there'd be nobody in the place. But that matinee, that's why it was packed and jammed. That band was working. Believe me. And we…

233.t: The first rehearsal in the closed tavern
233.s: The quartet set up on a Sunday and sounded like they had played together for years.
233.q: We went in there on a Sunday. They got there kind of late as to what was planned, according to plan. We were supposed to open on a Monday -- Sundays is off in Seattle -- it was dark.

112.t: Building the Nest band and the opening night
112.s: He assembles two saxophones, two trumpets and full rhythm, rehearses at home, and at opening the audience applauds instead of dancing.
112.q: : So anyhow, I started to get a band together. Now, I wasn't trying for sound, I was trying to get a band together to eat and make a living. But, by picking, by looking at the place, I said, well you certainly don't want no trombone in there. And you don't want too big a -- but yet, I had in mind…
